title: Near-duplicate detection across billions of items
prompt: You must find near-duplicate items in a corpus of billions. Which approach should anchor the matching strategy?
constraint: Billions of items — the method must scale sub-linearly, and a slight loss of recall is acceptable.

options.why: LSH hashes similar items into the same buckets so you only compare within buckets — sub-linear and purpose-built for near-duplicate detection at billion scale. The probabilistic bucketing trades a little recall for huge cost savings, which the constraint explicitly permits. Best fit.

ANN indexes (HNSW/IVF) are also sub-linear and tolerate the allowed recall loss, so this is defensible. But it adds an embedding model plus a vector index to build and tune, and it targets semantic similarity rather than the cheap near-exact dedup LSH delivers — heavier than the constraint requires.
O(n^2) over billions is quintillions of comparisons — the opposite of sub-linear. It maximizes recall the constraint says we don't need, at a cost that makes it infeasible at this scale. Rejected.

Sub-linear, and people do reach for it, but a single blocking key is brittle: any near-duplicate that differs on that key lands in a different block and is missed. That's a structural recall hole, not the bounded slight loss the constraint allows. Rejected.
